problem: The letter n is used twice with two different meanings. It is the time index in x[n], e[n], x̂[n], and it is also the number of bits per sample in 'an n-bit code word' and in the bit rate 'fs·n'. A student will read fs·n as 'sampling frequency times the time index'. The sampling frequency fs is also never defined.
fix: Use a separate symbol for bits per sample, for example R. Write: 'The quantizer replaces e[n] by one of L = 2^R levels and the encoder sends that level as an R-bit code word. The bit rate is fs·R bit/s, where fs is the sampling frequency in samples per second and R is the number of bits per sample.'

problem: The adder output is labelled x̂[n], but the adder output is the reconstructed sample x̃[n]. The predictor note 'x̂[n−1]' is also wrong: the predictor input is the reconstructed sample x̃[n−1] and its output is the prediction x̂[n]. This contradicts the x̂/x̃ notation used everywhere in the text.
fix: Label node i as x̃[n], and change the predictor note to 'x̂[n] = x̃[n−1]' (or 'in: x̃[n−1], out: x̂[n]'). Keep x̂ only for the prediction.

problem: The diagram shows one predictor fed from the receiver-side adder, with dashed edges crossing back to the transmitter subtractor. The text says the transmitter needs its own local decoder and predictor, but the figure does not show it, so the reader may think the prediction physically travels back over the channel.
fix: Label the predictor block as existing in both transmitter and receiver (for example 'Predictor (in Tx and Rx)') and note that the transmitter's copy is fed by its local adder, not by the receiver.

problem: 'The dashed feedback path in the figure is the reason DPCM stays stable' points at the wrong edges: the dashed edges carry the prediction, while the reconstructed sample travels on the solid edge from the adder to the predictor.
fix: Say instead: 'Because the quantizer sits inside the closed loop and the same q[n] is added on both sides, the transmitter and receiver predictors hold identical values, so quantizer noise does not accumulate.'
